text:
The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) have declared their Week 9 injury designations, and the Lions will be missing multiple starters, including one on offense, three on defense, and one not yet cleared from his injury list—all of which we knew ahead of time, based on coach Dan Campbell’s comments throughout the week.

Let’s look at Friday’s practice report and get you up to date on what we know.

Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded.

Ruled OUT

C Cade Mays (ankle) — Preparing for Juice Scruggs to start

EDGE DJ Wonnum (concussion)

LB Jack Campbell (neck)

CB D.J. Reed (hip)

S Kerby Joseph (knee, PUP) — Days remaining in injury evaluation clock: 11

Mays is dealing with a low ankle sprain, which typically keeps players out at least a week, and potentially as long as a month, so him being ruled out of this game was expected. How quickly he recovers is still to be determined, but the Lions have been highly fortunate to have Juice Scruggs stepping into the starting center role, and they’ve been planning on him starting since the beginning of this week.

Wonnum is still working through the NFL’s concussion protocols and won’t be able to return in time for this game. With head injury recovery times varying by individual, it’s unclear how long he will need before he is cleared. Second-round rookie Derrick Moore is expected to increase his role in Wonnum’s absence, and Campbell is seeing improvement:

“It was unfortunate we lost Wonnum, but yet, now (Moore) gets more reps. And the reps that he got are valuable, man. There’s no way to duplicate real in time game reps against good opponents and you see growth, you see growth. I saw growth in practice yesterday. So, the more he plays, the better he’s going to get. And we love where he’s going right now.”

Jack Campbell continues to improve, per Dan Campbell, but he should be considered out indefinitely until otherwise clarified.

“Jack continues to improve, which is all great news,” Dan Campbell said on Friday.

Reed said he felt good in the locker room following the game, but he was not cleared to practice this week and will miss this game. Campbell noted that he’s very confident with the team’s depth:

“(Ennis) Rakestraw is getting better. Rock (Ya-Sin) looks healthy and is playing good football. (Roger) McCreary, too. So, I just feel like these guys are starting to play pretty good football for us. And (Khalil) Dorsey, man, Dorsey’s contributing in a big way. So, I like where we’re at and it’s really a pretty depthwise, it’s a pretty strong room. So yeah, I don’t like the though of not having Reed, but at the same time, I’m encouraged. I’m encouraged. I think we’ll be OK here.”

Joseph is looking “better than anticipated,” according to safeties coach Jim O’Neil, but Campbell made it clear earlier in the week that the plan was to keep him out for another game, then continue to ramp up his participation levels next week, as he nears a return.

“It’s been great. Two weeks ago, it was classroom work, where we were really locked in. Then it was walkthrough and individual. Yesterday was his first team practice and he looked a lot better than what I anticipated him looking (like). So it was very encouraging. So now he’s gotta stack multiple days. He’s got to stack them, so today will be a big day for him, but he looked awesome yesterday at practice,” O’Neill said on Friday.

Questionable

RB Sione Vaki (ankle) — added to the injury report on Friday

RB Jacob Saylors (neck)

WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib)

Vaki was unexpectedly absent from Friday’s practice and has been given a questionable designation heading into this weekend’s game. Beyond that, the extent of his injury is unknown, and we may have to wait until Saturday—to see if he travels with the team—or even game time on Sunday, to find out his availability.

Saylors has dealt with a neck injury for two weeks and couldn’t finish Week 7’s game against the Vikings because of it. Look for the Lions to be cautious in his return, but with Vaki also questionable, the Lions could end up with a depth issue at running back.

St. Brown was injured in Week 7 but told the media on Thursday that, “I’m a little banged up, but I’ll be alright,” and is anticipating playing against the Dolphins.

Not listed with an injury designation

LB Amen Ogbongbemiga (toe)

CB Rock Ya-Sin (cramps)

S Brian Branch (concussion)

Ogbongbemiga was estimated to have been a limited participant on Wednesday and a full participant after that, and with him not carrying an injury designation, he should be good to go, giving the Lions special teams work and linebacker depth.

Ya-Sin dealt with cramps earlier in the week but still practiced in full each day. He’s potentially in line to challenge for a starting role this week with Reed sidelined.

Branch is nearing the end of the NFL’s concussion protocol, and Campbell said he expects him to be cleared and ready to play on Sunday.

“I think (Brian Branch) BB’s going to be good here. We’ll get through today, and I think we’ll be OK.”

title: Myles Garrett expected to return for Rams this weekend after 7-game injury absence.
description:
LOS ANGELES – Myles Garrett is expected to return for the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday at Washington after missing the past seven games with a knee injury.
“I’m just grateful that he’s back and that he’s feeling really good,” McVay said.
Garrett hasn't played since the Rams' season opener, when he made no tackles in their blowout loss to the 49ers in Australia.
Garrett underwent surgery after the Rams returned from Melbourne, and he was sidelined until he returned to practice this week.
Although Los Angeles is pressuring quarterbacks at a reasonable clip, the team is tied for 26th in the league with just 12 sacks, leading to frustration.
text:
LOS ANGELES – Myles Garrett is expected to return for the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday at Washington after missing the past seven games with a knee injury.

Coach Sean McVay announced Garrett's likely availability, barring a late setback, on Friday before practice. The Rams (4-4) acquired Garrett in a trade with Cleveland over the summer, but the two-time AP NFL Defensive Player of the Year has played in just one game for his new team.

“I’m just grateful that he’s back and that he’s feeling really good,” McVay said.

Garrett hasn't played since the Rams' season opener, when he made no tackles in their blowout loss to the 49ers in Australia. Afterward, Garrett revealed he wasn't fully fit due to a knee injury that limited him throughout training camp.

Garrett underwent surgery after the Rams returned from Melbourne, and he was sidelined until he returned to practice this week. Those seven weeks were the longest injury absence of his 10-year NFL career.

“It was very difficult, (because) this is what I love to do,” Garrett said. “I love being around my teammates, being able to help the whole group shine. Seeing them going out there and having fun, it's like I want to be there in those moments and share in their success. Not being able to do what I feel like I was put here to do, it hurt me for a while. But I've got a good team around me. I've got a great family. Blessed to be in a great place with great weather, so I'm happy to be back.”

After months of anticipation, Rams fans should finally get to see Garrett playing alongside Aaron Donald against the Commanders. A three-time Defensive Player of the Year, Donald was tempted out of his 2 1/2-year retirement by the Rams’ acquisition of Garrett, but he didn’t make the trip to Australia while ramping up his fitness.

“I think offenses really have to pick their poison,” Garrett said with a smile. “Who’s going to be freed up on this play? And I think either of us are pretty good at winning one-on-ones, so we’re going to have some fun.”

Garrett said his knee injury didn't happen on a single event or play, but instead “cascaded” late in training camp before getting even worse in Melbourne.

“There were just some hitches in my gait,” Garrett said. “There were just things I was dealing with mechanically that just only continued to evolve, or I guess worsen, as I played more throughout that game.”

McVay acknowledged that the Rams will examine whether Garrett should have had his surgery earlier in the year, but they're busy looking forward to what they can do with Garrett and Donald leading the way.

“You always want to reflect back on what we would do differently,” McVay said.

The Rams' pass rush hasn't been great in Garrett's absence. Although Los Angeles is pressuring quarterbacks at a reasonable clip, the team is tied for 26th in the league with just 12 sacks, leading to frustration.

“We keep attacking, but we're not finishing off all the plays,” said edge rusher Byron Young, who leads the Rams with 4 1/2 sacks. “I think we've been getting good pressure, but not getting the quarterback down and finishing games ... Having MG back will help that for sure.”

Terrance Ferguson also had been expected to return to the Rams' lineup against Washington after missing the past five games with an ankle sprain, but the second-year tight end was ruled out Friday afternoon after apparently injuring his hamstring during their final practice.

While Garrett likely returns to the defense's front line, the Rams' secondary is hurting.

Jaylen Watson is out for the season with a shoulder injury, and fellow starting cornerback Trent McDuffie missed the entire week of practice with a back injury. McDuffie is questionable for Sunday, as is starting safety Kam Curl, who has a foot injury.

title: What's the Cost of an NFL Injury? - Kellogg Insight
description:

text:
It’s a common refrain among football fans: we could’ve been contenders if it weren’t for the injuries.

But the impact of injuries on NFL teams is a question that has never been fully quantified, says Joel Shapiro, a clinical associate professor of managerial economics and decision sciences at Kellogg.

“There’s a lot of very incomplete information out there about how much injuries matter,” says Shapiro. “How much, if at all, should teams care about whether a player is available to play or not?”

So Shapiro set out to create his own new metric that measures the cost of a player’s injury on their team. His metric, which he calls “Percent Cash Wasted,” takes an economic approach, calculating how much of a team’s payroll is sidelined due to injury each season.

When he applied the metric to over 350 NFL teams’ seasons from 2012 to 2022, he confirmed that injuries do make a difference to a team’s success. But the magnitude of that impact doesn’t match the common wisdom inside and outside football organizations.

“Losing payroll due to injury isn’t as big a deal as a lot of people would have thought,” says Shapiro. “But that’s with one probable exception: highly paid quarterbacks.”

Economics on the gridiron

Though the impact of injuries may seem like a matter for coaches and athletic trainers, Shapiro argues that it, like a lot of questions in sports, boils down to economics.

Teams have a finite amount of resources to spend in constructing their roster. In the NFL, that limit is defined by the salary cap, which governs how much each team can spend on its players each season.

“One of the most important things that any executive does, in sports or otherwise, is figure out how to allocate capital,” Shapiro says.

To find an edge in this system, organizations need to accurately value the different components of their team and distribute their budget accordingly. Invest in a top-tier offensive line, for example, and you may have less money to attract high-end linebackers.

And then there are injuries, the wild card that can throw the most-carefully laid roster strategy into chaos. In a contact sport like football, injuries are an expected part of the game; in Shapiro’s data sample, when you total up all seasons from all players, one out of three included at least one game missed due to injury.

Football analysts have tried to quantify the impact of these injuries on team performance through metrics such as Adjusted Games Lost or Wins Above Replacement-Adjusted Injuries Lost. Both of these approaches weigh injuries to starters and valuable players more heavily, acknowledging that losing a star quarterback is not the same as losing a third-string tight end.

But Shapiro felt that an important piece was still missing from these stats: the cost, in dollars, of losing that player’s on-field performance.

“That’s what this study is all about, trying to understand how player injury affects decisions that teams should make around resource allocation,” Shapiro says. “I wanted to bring together the economic impact of injury and winning in a way that I hadn’t seen done before.”

Waste not, win more?

In an age of complex, AI-driven sports analysis, Shapiro’s Percent Cash Wasted metric sticks to basic math. It involves multiplying a player’s salary per game by the number of games missed due to injury, divided by the team’s total payroll.

For example, if a player is making $10 million a season and missed 30 percent of games, that’s $3 million wasted. At the current NFL salary cap of roughly $300 million, that’s 1 percent of a standard payroll lost. Tally up these figures across the roster and you get a team-wide figure for how much of its season’s payroll went to players unable to play.

In Shapiro’s data sample, teams’ Percent Cash Wasted ranged from as low as 1.1 percent to as high as 28.8 percent. On average, teams lost close to 10 percent of their payroll to injury each year—lower than many would predict, Shapiro says.

“You ask the public to guess, [and] they’ll say, ‘I don’t know, 30 percent?’” he says. “Even executives were guessing 15 percent to 20 percent.”

And as might be expected, less payroll lost to injury correlates with higher success—but only slightly higher. Winning a single extra game during the regular season aligned with roughly a 7 percentage point reduction in Percent Cash Wasted.

“In order to win one more game, an average team losing 10 percent of their payroll to injury would have to bring that all the way down to about 3 percent,” Shapiro says. “Which means that the depth that teams have gravitated to in this 11-year period that I looked at seems to be doing a pretty good job.”

In other words, the drop-off in quality from an injured starter to their backup isn’t hugely significant for a team’s success. But that rule has one big exception: star quarterbacks.

In Shapiro’s sample, there were five cases where a quarterback who cost more than 5 percent of a team’s total payroll was lost to a significant injury (Hurts’s salary is roughly 10 percent of the Eagles’ 2026 cap). In all five cases, those teams won far fewer games than their preseason expectations—and saw a deeper decline than would be expected if the same loss happened in any other position.

“All five teams completely tanked, which makes sense because of the importance of the quarterback to the team,” Shapiro says.

Better decision-making

In a post-Moneyball sports world where new stats arrive constantly, the best metrics are the ones that help teams make smarter decisions and get the edge on their competition, according to Shapiro.

“If your lever is money, and your goal is winning, and you want to spend money to win, then knowing the impact of injury absolutely can determine and should determine how you spend those dollars,” he says.

But front offices might draw opposing conclusions from Shapiro’s findings. Some might be more inclined to sign talented but injury-prone players, knowing that their time off the field won’t be as damaging as expected. Others might conclude that backups aren’t a significant drop-off in quality from starters and avoid giving big contracts to stars other than quarterbacks.

“Is talent really worth the premium that teams pay for it?” Shapiro asks. “I’m not sure which strategy is the right answer yet.”

In the meantime, Shapiro is interested in testing his Percent Cash Wasted metric in other sports, or maybe even in non-sports economic contexts.

“The resources that you spend on individuals who aren’t contributing is an interesting concept,” Shapiro says. “Lack of productivity and lack of availability are different things. But this notion of how efficient we are with our resources—that could be transferable to other settings.”

text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Miami Dolphins left guard Kadyn Proctor will play in Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions, coach Jeff Hafley said, after clearing concussion protocol.

Proctor displayed concussion symptoms following the Dolphins' win over the New York Jets in Week 7 and subsequently missed their loss to the New England Patriots in Week 8. He returned to the practice field Wednesday and was a full participant in each of the team's practices this week.

Hafley told reporters that the rookie officially exited the league's return to participation protocol Friday, and he was cleared for Sunday's game.

His absence was felt last week, as the Dolphins struggled to run the ball against a stout New England defense. They averaged a season-low 1.74 yards before contact per rush attempt, down from 3.09 yards before contact in their six previous games with Proctor in the lineup.

Offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik said last week was "probably our first game" where the Dolphins' blocking kept them from better production in the run game, and commended fill-in starter Jarrett Kingston for bouncing back after a slow start to the game. Running back Ollie Gordon II was also complimentary of Kingston but said the team will "get back to being us" with Proctor back in the lineup.

"When Proctor's out there, you can feel his presence out there on most every play," Slowik said. "He's just a massive guy who can move, he displaces people. He's putting defensive tackles five, six yards down the field. He caps off at the end of plays. We throw the ball 10 yards down the field for a 30-yard explosive and next thing you know, Proctor's showing up on the screen and everyone's like 'Where'd he come from.' You know what I mean?

"He just gives everybody a lot of energy when he's out there, and that's not even including what you can do with him scheme-wise."

The 6-foot-7, 360-pound Proctor was the 13th overall pick in this year's draft, and the first player taken under first-year general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan. Despite playing left tackle at Alabama, Proctor has exclusively played left guard for the Dolphins this season, where he lines up next to 6-foot-7, 325-pound left tackle Patrick Paul.

The pairing has paid off in the run game; Miami averages 6.2 yards per rush on inside runs toward the left side of the field, including 3.87 yards before first contact -- good for third-most and second-most in the NFL, respectively. The Dolphins also lead the league with 23% of their carries to that side going for 10 or more yards.

NFL news, live updates: Rams' Myles Garrett reportedly in line to return Sunday; Ravens finalize trade for Jacoby Brissett after TNF disaster

We're officially into Week 9 of the NFL season (and the looming NFL trade deadline), where teams will have to make a decision on the intended course of the remainder of their season — are they going all in? Or is it time to tear it all down and look toward the future?

After falling to 4-5 on Thursday night, the Baltimore Ravens finalized a trade for Jacoby Brissett as they look to salvage their season. The team officially placed Lamar Jackson (thumb) and Tyler Huntley (toe) on injured reserve this week, and undrafted free agent Joe Fagnano looked like … well, an undrafted free agent in his first career start. He completed 10-of-18 pass attempts for 60 yards with two picks against the Jacksonville Jaguars, logging a 22.7 passer rating along the way. Despite Brissett's struggles this season, there's no doubt he'll be a welcome upgrade.

NFL fans also await news on the fate of star running back Jonathan Taylor, who has been touted as a potential trade-deadline mover as the Indianapolis Colts kicked off their franchise reset with a fire sale. They've already traded away two foundational players, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, for several draft picks as they look to the future, leaving us to wonder whether Taylor could be next.

The Los Angeles Rams could be a deadline buyer, as they've won back-to-back games and are reportedly already getting a long-awaited midseason reinforcement in the form of edge rusher Myles Garrett, a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and the league's single-season sack record holder.

Garrett's in line for a return to game action on the road Sunday against the Washington Commanders, according to NFL Network's Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport. Coming back from early-season knee surgery that landed him on injured reserve, Garrett has practiced all week.

text:
This week, members of the Detroit Lions roster, including the linebackers unit, have been reflecting on the impact of seeing one of their leaders and teammates being carted off the field against the Minnesota Vikings.

Cognitively, players understand the inherent risk of playing a violent sport. Still, nothing can prepare an individual when a player is lying face down and motionless on the field.

Many expressed that while the group must quickly turn the page, they are still keeping Jack Campbell at the forefront of their thoughts.

Derrick Barnes expressed to local reporters this week the jarring scene at Ford Field has forced him to contemplate if he wants his young son to even play the game of football.

Barnes expressed, via the Detroit Free Press, “I don’t think you’re playing football. Right after I said that, he’s like, ‘Daddy, I play football. Daddy, I play football.' So, I’m like, ‘We’re going to have a long conversation. I want to tell you the great things about it and the bad things about it and you make that decision if you really want to.’ But no, I told him, I said, ‘Man, don’t worry about it. We’re going to get you into some baseball, man. Some golf.’ Things I wish I’d have done. Especially golf. Things I wish I would have got to as a young kid.”

The team is preparing this week with a fighters mentality, knowing that Campbell would not want the group sulking or feeling down for him, given what he is going to be facing over the next several weeks and months.

"Jack’s a fighter, we all know Jack and knowing Jack, he wants us to keep going throughout our day. That’s why we all love Jack, humble guy, so to hear the news from Coach this morning was awesome. It was a sigh of relief," linebacker Malcolm Rodriguez said. "Obviously he’s progressing better. It’s one of those things where he’s going to keep fighting. I know he wants to come back and play already. It’s just how Jack is and that’s why all the guys in here love him."

title: Myles Garrett's return could unleash Aaron Donald and lift an injury-hit Rams defense
description:
LOS ANGELES -- Myles Garrett trotted out of the Los Angeles Rams facility and onto the green grass for his first practice in nearly two months, and Byron Young couldn't contain himself.
McDuffie himself is fighting to get back on the field after he injured his back in Sunday's 24-9 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers.
Just one year ago, Los Angeles finished tied for seventh in the league with 47 sacks.

That's where having Garrett, Donald and McDuffie playing together for the first time could pay dividends -- so long as Garrett and McDuffie are healthy.
text:
LOS ANGELES -- Myles Garrett trotted out of the Los Angeles Rams facility and onto the green grass for his first practice in nearly two months, and Byron Young couldn't contain himself.

"Get your cameras ready!" Young shouted. "I'm so happy to see this."

Garrett spent the beginning of Thursday's practice chatting and trading jokes with Aaron Donald, who ended a two-year retirement this summer in part for a moment like the one coming. After a career of double-teams, he wanted to share a defensive line with another multi-time Defensive Player of the Year. Whenever that time would come, the Rams would feature the first defensive line in NFL history with two players with at least 100 career sacks and a 20-sack season under their belt.

This was the delayed euphoria, expanding like a balloon that was ready to burst. Not only have the Rams waited months since a blockbuster trade to see the real version of their two-time Defensive Player of the Year in a game-week setting, but they also needed a reprieve from the avalanche that continues to fall on their heads.

Garrett's status for Sunday against the Washington Commanders remains to be seen, but his return to practice came in a week filled with more injury chaos. On the day Los Angeles decided to start the practice window for Garrett, who has missed seven straight games after knee surgery, the team placed cornerback Jaylen Watson on season-ending injured reserve with a shoulder injury. That means the Rams won't play a snap this season with the four acquisitions they brought in to level up the defense -- Garrett, Donald, Watson and two-time All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie -- on the field at the same time.

McDuffie himself is fighting to get back on the field after he injured his back in Sunday's 24-9 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. He's missed two practices this week in the attempt to heal.

The roller coaster of emotions on one side of the ball contains a conundrum as Week 9 approaches for this 4-4 team:

The Rams' defense has a chance to be special, but it also has to overcome so much to be so.

"I've been the coach for 10 years, and I know '22 was a season that we had a lot of injuries, particularly at the offensive line," coach Sean McVay said, "but this has been more than any year, including '22, with the amount of guys out at different spots that are key and critical to your identities."

The Rams have to overcome the loss of Watson, whose nine pass deflections, erasures with press-man coverage and stout run defense have set a new tone for a secondary that badly needed one after last season's playoff slide. They will look to Josh Wallace and Emmanuel Forbes Jr. for help, and both could wind up playing on the perimeter if McDuffie misses more time. Enough is up in the air that the Rams added eighth-year veteran David Long Jr. to the practice squad for insurance.

They also have to continue to absorb the losses of nose tackle Poona Ford and defensive end Kobie Turner. Ford is out for the season, and the replacement tandem of Ty Hamilton and Tyler Davis helped shut down the Las Vegas Raiders and Chargers for 112 combined rushing yards on 2.7 yards per carry the past two weeks. The run defense has improved over the past two weeks, in part because the Rams faced struggling run games and in part because of the rise of linebacker Omar Speights.

But Garrett can provide an antidote to so many of the concerns if he can get back to form. He plays in the edge spot Turner does on base downs, where he can set a similar edge with his 272-pound frame. Turner has to miss the next two games while on injured reserve with a groin injury.

But it's when the Rams force teams into throwing the ball that Garrett will make up the most ground. He joins a team tied for 26th in the NFL with 12 sacks. Just one year ago, Los Angeles finished tied for seventh in the league with 47 sacks. That same season, with the Cleveland Browns, Garrett had 23 on his lonesome for the most in a season in NFL history.

Garrett's injury created a double blow to the pass rush, as the Rams sent Jared Verse to the Browns to get him. Verse finished last season with 7 1/2 sacks and led the team with a 17.5 percent pressure rate, according to Sports Info Solutions. Garrett was here to supercharge his role of commanding double-teams and chip blocks while collapsing the blind side of the pocket to chase quarterbacks to the right, where Byron Young could chase them down with his speed.

Young leads the Rams this season with 4 1/2 sacks and a 14.7 percent pressure rate, but he's trying to get back to and then exceed last season's totals of 12 sacks and a 15.5 percent pressure rate, which landed him in his first Pro Bowl.

"We were doing a get-off (in practice), and I was like, 'Boy, I've missed that,'" Young said. "I feel like we've been getting good pressure, but we're not getting the quarterback down. That happened a few games ago, and that's something we don't live by. We live by getting after the quarterback and getting him down and finishing games.

"Having him be back, I'm looking for that to help us along the way. All of the attention he's going to cause by getting to the QB, I'm looking forward to it."

But the biggest beneficiary of a healthy Garrett would be Donald. After all, the prospect of rushing as a secondary option in the eyes of opposing offensive lines is what became so enticing about a comeback. That has largely disappeared with Josaiah Stewart in Garrett's place, but the math dilemma can return on offensive lines trying to divvy up resources on the same side of the line Garrett and Donald play on.

"He's looking good, looking fast," Donald said of Garrett. "(We're) getting to work with him in full pads and playing off each other. It looked pretty good today, so I'm excited about having him here, having him back, and seeing what we do Sunday."

And if that comes together, the Rams have a way to ease the burden on their outside cornerbacks. They have reason to be optimistic about Wallace, given the surge he's shown in his third season. He's playing outside more than ever, and he's allowed just six of 20 passes against him to be completed for a total of 77 yards and no touchdowns, according to SIS. Only one cornerback in the NFL has allowed less than his 3.9 yards per coverage snap allowed on at least 20 targets, and that's his teammate McDuffie at 3.3.

The Rams will likely dial up their use of zone looks without Watson's press-man presence. That can allow the secondary to play downhill and with eyes on the quarterback. Safety Quentin Lake is tied for second in the league with three interceptions, and McDuffie is one behind him with two despite two missed games. But the real boost could come to free safety Kam Kinchens, who had six interceptions across his first two seasons but has yet to get his hands on one this season.

The path is there for the Rams to rise from a high-floor defense to an impactful one. They rank No. 5 in the league in yards allowed and No. 12 in points but are in the bottom 10 in sacks and takeaways. That's where having Garrett, Donald and McDuffie playing together for the first time could pay dividends -- so long as Garrett and McDuffie are healthy.

That's why the building has a swirl of emotions right now.

text:
Kyler Murray’s hamstring injury is serious enough that it will sideline him for at least a week.

Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell told reporters in his Thursday press conference that Murray is out for Monday night’s game against the Bills with a hamstring strain and is considered week-to-week.

Carson Wentz will start Week 9, which will be his second start of the season.

“For [Murray], his movement skills, and the way he plays the game, we do feel like we’d be putting him at risk of possibly turning this into a more significant injury than it is by trying to have him work through it here early on,” O’Connell said. “So, Carson will start the football game and Max [Brosmer] will back him up.”

While it didn’t seem like O’Connell was too concerned about Murray’s availability earlier in the week, further testing revealed the extent of the issue.

“I think hamstrings are always unique,” O’Connell said. "[Y]ou always have to understand that whatever that picture or that imaging says, sometimes it’s an injury you can really hone in on. That’s why I wanted to be certain before I went speculating on Monday just because I wanted to be sure it wasn’t something that would prohibit him from playing — until it was.

“I’m not going to get into the details of the grade or the injury or the level medically speaking, but just knowing that Kyler needs his mobility — it’s a big, huge part of what makes him an effective player. If that puts him at risk of potentially adding to the grade of the injury, we can’t do that. It’s a long season. We hope to get him back and get him going.”

O’Connell noted injured reserve is not a consideration for Murray with this injury.

Wentz stepped in and played after Murray suffered a concussion earlier this season. Wentz completed 23-of-39 passes against the Packers and Bears for 276 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions.

“Obviously, there’s a ton of confidence in Carson,” O’Connell said. “He’s had a major, major role in two wins this year against two really good teams. He’s a steadying presence and a guy we know can go in and play good football, that’s why we feel so great about having him here.

“He’s going to throw a lot of completions. He’s going to put the ball in play. He’s got such a high, high understanding of not only the offense but what he’s looking at on the other side. He has 100 games of experience. He’s the perfect guy in a moment where you can’t have Kyler out there at full strength to go in there. And we feel very strongly about when Carson’s in there, we’re going to get really effective quarterback play.”

Minnesota’s offense has struggled to generate yards and points this season, with the club ranking No. 27 in scoring and No. 29 in total yards. We’ll see if Wentz can provide a spark to change that on Monday night.

text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- The Minnesota Vikings have once again hopped on their quarterback carousel. Backup Carson Wentz will start Monday night's game against the Buffalo Bills, coach Kevin O'Connell announced Thursday, because starter Kyler Murray is nursing a strained hamstring.

The change marks the 14th time the Vikings have shifted from one quarterback to another during a season, either because of injuries or for performance reasons, since Kirk Cousins tore his right Achilles tendon midway through the 2023 season.

"I've enjoyed being here," Wentz said. "I enjoy this offense, enjoy this team, enjoy working with [O'Connell] and I'm excited for another opportunity."

Murray suffered the injury while running on a read-option play early in the fourth quarter of the Vikings' 19-15 loss Sunday to the Detroit Lions. Murray also struggled to connect with open receivers throughout the game, leaving receiver Justin Jefferson so frustrated that he declined to speak with reporters afterward.

O'Connell said that putting Murray on injured reserve is not a consideration.

"I don't believe it to be much more than a week-to-week kind of thing right now," O'Connell said. "But for him, his movement skills and the way he plays the game, we do feel like we'd be putting him at risk of possibly turning this into a more significant injury than it is by trying to have him work through it here early on."

Murray scrambled seven times during a Week 4 game against the New Orleans Saints but has run only 13 times in his five remaining starts. O'Connell said the injury would affect more than simply his ability to run.

"It's more the explosive movements, the quick-twitch movements," O'Connell said. "Running is obviously a part of some of that ... but it's more of just the overall ability to impact the game. And ultimately, we could try to say all we want of, 'Hey, you can play, but you just got to stay in the pocket.' But then football starts, and it's an imperfect game where he's going to react and we don't want to make this strain any worse than it is."

Murray missed most of two games earlier this season because of a concussion, and his QBR (44.7) ranks No. 26 out of 30 qualified quarterbacks as he plays on a one-year contract. Speaking Monday, O'Connell said that Murray would remain his starter this week if he were healthy. Asked Thursday if Wentz had an opportunity to earn additional starts based on his performance, independent of Murray's health, O'Connell said in part: "It's all about this week for our team."

Wentz has started six games and played most of a seventh since signing with the Vikings in August 2025. The team is 4-3 in those games during which Wentz has completed 63.9% of his passes for 1,492 yards, nine touchdowns and five interceptions.

He has excelled in getting the ball to Jefferson, however. In those seven games, Jefferson has caught 44 passes for 615 yards and two touchdowns.

"[Wentz] is the perfect guy in a moment where you can't have Kyler out there at full strength to go in there," O'Connell said. "And we feel very strongly about when Carson's in there, we're going to get really effective quarterback play."

Patriots injury report, Thursday
text:
The Green Bay Packers made two adjustments to the Week 9 injury report on Thursday: cornerback Keisean Nixon was downgraded and running back MarShawn Lloyd was added.

Nixon did not practice on Thursday while dealing with a groin injury. He was listed as limited on Wednesday. The veteran has not missed a game since signing with the Packers before the 2022 season, but he might need to practice Friday to have a realistic chance of playing Sunday against the New England Patriots.

Lloyd, who suffered through two injury-plagued seasons to start his NFL career, has his first injury of 2026: a knee injury. He was limited on Thursday. It's possible the Packers could return Chris Brooks this week, providing depth at running back if Lloyd can't go.

In addition to Nixon, the Packers did not have Zaire Franklin, Sean Rhyan, Travis Glover or Josh Whyle at Thursday's practice. All five are in danger of not playing against the Patriots.

Micah Parsons practiced in a limited capacity for the second straight day after returning on Wednesday. The Packers were in pads on Thursday. Parsons is not expected to play until Week 12 at the earliest.

The Patriots made three changes: defensive lineman Christian Barmore practiced after missing Wednesday with an illness, while the team added cornerback Marcus Jones (foot) and safety Brenden Schooler (hamstring) to the injury report with new injuries. Receiver A.J. Brown didn't practice for the second straight day, so it's possible the Packers will be down a starting corner while the Patriots will be down two starting receivers (including former Packer Romeo Doubs, who is on injured reserve).

The Packers and Patriots will have final practices on Friday before issuing status designations on the final injury report.

text:
Despite a 6-1 record, Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray's starting job is in question due to poor offensive performance.

New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo is dealing with a hamstring injury, leading to a potential backfield shakeup.

The Minnesota Vikings sit atop the NFC North with a 6-1 record, but quarterback Kyler Murray will miss the team’s showdown against the Buffalo Bills on Monday Night Football with a hamstring injury and faces mounting questions about his long-term job security.

The Vikings’ winning record masks a subpar offense that ranks 27th in the league, averaging just 20 points per game. Production relies heavily on a dominant defense allowing a league-low 13.3 points per game, rather than a potent passing attack.

Murray looks uncomfortable in head coach Kevin O’Connell’s system, where the former Arizona Cardinals’ franchise quarterback has thrown for just 1,022 yards, five touchdowns and three interceptions through six games while struggling with downfield consistency and timing.

Murray’s hold on the position is tenuous.

The Vikings’ front office limited its financial risk by signing him to a low-cost, one-year “prove-it” contract, leaving the franchise with no long-term obligation if his subpar play persists. Speculation is intensifying following a Week 8 loss to the Detroit Lions, especially with Murray ruled out for Week 9.

Carson Wentz could secure the starting job permanently.

Cam Skattebo injury sparks Giants backfield shakeup

Cam Skattebo remains central to the New York Giants’ plans, but a lingering hamstring injury complicates his availability heading into a Week 9 road game against the reeling Philadelphia Eagles.

The former Arizona State running back was limited to side work with trainers after exacerbating the injury on Oct. 25 during an explosive overtime run against Houston. The Giants had a bye last week. John Harbaugh characterized Skattebo’s status as day-to-day.

Skattebo hadn't practiced as of Thursday morning, Nov. 5.

The backfield crunch is amplified by Tyrone Tracy Jr. landing on injured reserve with a hamstring strain. With Tracy sidelined for at least four games, veteran Devin Singletary projects to carry the bulk of the workload if Skattebo is limited. The Giants also signed Greg Desrosiers Jr. off the Los Angeles Chargers’ practice squad to the active roster.

Seahawks integrate Quenton Nelson after Colts selloff

The Seattle Seahawks are reshaping their offensive line after acquiring left guard Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts.

Seattle sent a third-round selection and a 2028 fifth-round pick to Indianapolis to secure the elite blocker, who made his Seahawks debut in a loss to the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football. Analysts expect Seattle to offset the draft-capital loss with future compensatory picks.

Nelson provides immediate protection for the reigning Super Bowl champs, who have ruled out quarterback Sam Darnold for their Week 9 game against the Cardinals. Drew Lock is expected to start.

Nelson should also help open running lanes for Jadarian Price, Zach Charbonnet, Emanuel Wilson and George Holani.

Rashee Rice solidifies role in Chiefs’ passing game

Rashee Rice returned to play last week against the Denver Broncos after missing two games with a strained right hamstring and a lingering knee injury.

The wide receiver immediately re-energized a stagnant offense, hauling in seven of his eight targets for 53 yards and a touchdown. His presence ended a glaring drought for Patrick Mahomes, who had failed to throw a touchdown pass during Rice’s two-week absence.

Kansas City fell to its division rival, 28–24, marking the team’s second consecutive loss. But Rice’s health and immediate production provided a critical silver lining as the Chiefs prepare for a Week 9 matchup against the New York Jets.

Purdy maintains MVP pace despite Niners injuries

Brock Purdy keeps his offense operating at an elite level despite a persistent wave of injuries to his supporting cast.

The Gilbert Perry grad protects the football, avoids sacks with precise pocket movement and delivers accurate throws under pressure. His ability to elevate the roster keeps him at the forefront of the NFL MVP conversation entering Week 9, along with Buffalo Bills superstar Josh Allen, despite dealing with an injury-depleted receiving corps.

Purdy led the 49ers to a 6–1 start before their Week 8 bye. Through his first seven games, he has completed 69.2% of his passes for 1,748 yards, racking up 15 passing touchdowns against just four interceptions. He also has a league-leading 79.3 QBR and an impressive 110.1 passer rating. The Niners host the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
